title: CCNP ENARSI: Route-Map Filtering & Prefix Redistribution
description: R1 is redistributing internal subnets into BGP using route-map EXPORT_BGP. An unintended deny sequence or missing permit statement is causing critical subnet 192.168.10.0/24 to be dropped. Troubleshoot the route-map and restore route propagation to R2.
objective: Correct the route-map statement on R1 so that 192.168.10.0/24 is permitted and advertised to R2 via BGP.

hints.title: Level 1: Directional Hint
hints.content: Check 'show route-map EXPORT_BGP' and 'show ip access-list' on R1 to see what prefixes match the policy.

hints.title: Level 2: Protocol Mechanics
hints.content: Route-maps have an implicit 'deny' at the end. If a prefix is not explicitly permitted by a sequence number, or if an ACL referenced by a permit sequence denies it, the prefix is filtered.

hints.title: Level 3: Technical Fix
hints.content: On R1, permit 192.168.10.0/24 in the referenced prefix-list or add 'route-map EXPORT_BGP permit 20' matching prefix 192.168.10.0/24.

checks.description: Prefix 192.168.10.0/24 present in R2 BGP table

viewpointQuestions.question: Why was prefix 192.168.10.0/24 dropped even though R1 had an active network statement for it?
viewpointQuestions.answer: R1 had outbound policy 'neighbor 10.1.1.2 route-map EXPORT_BGP out'. In Cisco IOS XE, route-maps and prefix-lists conclude with an implicit 'deny all'. Sequence 10 of route-map EXPORT_BGP matched prefix-list PERMITTED_NETS which only contained 192.168.20.0/24. Because 192.168.10.0/24 was not matched by any permit sequence, it hit the implicit deny and was filtered.

viewpointQuestions.question: What is the key advantage of an IP prefix-list over an IP Access Control List (ACL) for BGP policy routing?
viewpointQuestions.answer: 1) Performance: Prefix-lists use a binary tree data structure for lookup, significantly faster than sequential ACL evaluation on large routing tables. 2) Prefix length flexibility: Prefix-lists allow the 'ge' (greater than or equal) and 'le' (less than or equal) parameters to match a subnet mask length range without complex wildcard calculations.

viewpointQuestions.question: How does Cisco IOS evaluate multiple match clauses on the same line vs separate lines in a route-map?
viewpointQuestions.answer: Match statements on the SAME line are evaluated with a logical OR (e.g. 'match ip address 1 2' matches ACL 1 OR ACL 2). Match statements on DIFFERENT lines within the same sequence are evaluated with a logical AND (e.g. 'match ip address 1' and 'match metric 10' requires both conditions to match).

examPracticeCommands.purpose: Inspect route-map sequences, permit/deny actions, match/set clauses, and match packet counters.
examPracticeCommands.examTip: On the 300-410 ENARSI exam, always check the sequence numbers to ensure more specific match statements precede general ones.

examPracticeCommands.purpose: Verify sequence entries, exact prefixes, ge/le length limits, and match hit counts.
examPracticeCommands.examTip: Hit counts reveal whether routing updates are actively matching the intended prefix-list sequence.

examPracticeCommands.purpose: Verify the exact outbound prefixes sent to a BGP peer after route-map policies are applied.
examPracticeCommands.examTip: This is the most definitive command to verify whether a route-map filtered an advertised prefix.

examPracticeCommands.purpose: Trigger dynamic route refresh and policy re-evaluation without dropping TCP peering sessions.
examPracticeCommands.examTip: Always use soft reconfiguration or route refresh in production and exam scenarios to prevent session resets.
